Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Being reminded of the event by others

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
I have to be on guard all the time
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The appraisal of permanent bodily damage is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma context. The other selected items consistently reflect ongoing external danger and hyperarousal (world dangerous, on guard, startle, false alarms, threat in silence) plus intrusive sensory memory, but there are no corroborating memory, threat, or strategy items indicating injury-focused trauma consequences, pain, disability, or body-related threat. For a refugee trauma profile, this isolated somatic-damage belief is not impossible, but in this item set it stands out as clinically incoherent with the dominant formulation of danger-based threat and avoidance.

vignette: Mark, a 21-year-old European male, works as a Public Defender and is currently in a relationship. His traumatic experience as a refugee has deeply affected his life and mental health. Mark's daily routine is marked by constant vigilance and an overwhelming sense of danger that stems from the harrowing experiences he endured during his journey to safety. The trauma began when Mark was forced to flee his war-torn homeland, leaving behind everything familiar. The memories of the violence and chaos are vivid, often replaying in flashes of images and bodily sensations that feel almost real. These visual memories, combined with the physical reenactment he experiences when they surface, have left him feeling perpetually on edge. Even now, Mark finds himself jumping at ordinary sounds or reacting to unusual silence as if danger is looming. Mark's belief that "the world is a dangerous place" has become a constant narrative in his mind. This negative appraisal drives much of his behavior and thought patterns. He constantly monitors his own thoughts for signs of going crazy, fearing that the trauma will consume him completely. The intense emotions he feels without clear images further reinforce this sense of danger, leading to an almost obsessive need for control. The recurrence of these memories has become so overwhelming that Mark avoids talking about them with others, including his partner and colleagues. He finds it easier to keep silent rather than relive the trauma through conversation or be reminded by someone else's accounts. This avoidance not only isolates him but also amplifies his fears, as he believes sharing might make things worse. Mark's hypervigilance and constant vigilance have taken a toll on his work as a Public Defender. He finds it difficult to fully engage in court proceedings or consultations with clients because the slightest sound can trigger a startling response. This has led to moments of disconnection, where he momentarily feels his body is reliving the trauma, making it hard for him to focus and be present. The false alarms Mark experiences further exacerbate his hypervigilance. He often reacts as if he is in immediate danger even when there's no real threat. This cycle of fear and heightened alertness has made it difficult for him to trust his surroundings or those around him, leading to a persistent sense that something dangerous is about to happen. His partner has noticed the changes in Mark's behavior but struggles to understand the depth of his fears. The avoidance and hyperarousal have strained their relationship, as Mark often finds himself withdrawing into his own thoughts to protect himself from being overwhelmed by external triggers. His belief that he must constantly be on guard because "you never know what can happen next" has become a self-perpetuating cycle. Mark finally sought help when the intensity of these symptoms began to affect his ability to perform at work and maintain his relationships. He was certain that if he didn't address these feelings, they would continue to consume him completely. What frightened him most was the fear of losing control and the belief that the trauma would never truly leave him. In therapy, Mark hopes to find ways to manage his hypervigilance and reduce the frequency of false alarms. He is seeking strategies to cope with the vivid memories and emotional intensity without feeling overwhelmed by them. His goal is to regain a sense of safety and control in his daily life, both personally and professionally.
